content: Cabbage, scientifically known as Brassica oleracea (Capitata Group), belongs to the family Brassicaceae (also known as Cruciferae). It is a herbaceous, biennial, dicotyledonous flowering plant characterized by its leaves forming a dense, compact cluster. Cabbages cultivated in late autumn and early winter are referred to as coleworts. The plant is derived from a leafy wild mustard species native to the Mediterranean region. The English word cabbage originates from the Norman-Picard term caboche, meaning head. The modern cabbage was developed through artificial selection aimed at reducing the length of the internodes. The dense core of the cabbage is called the babchka. Cabbage is closely related to the turnip. The sharp or bitter taste sometimes associated with cabbage is due to the presence of glucosinolates. The edible part of the cabbage plant is the leafy head, specifically the spherical cluster of immature leaves, excluding the partially unfolded outer leaves. This cabbage head is widely consumed in various forms, including raw, cooked, or preserved, and is a popular leaf vegetable. Raw Consumption Raw cabbage is typically sliced into thin strips or shredded for use in salads, such as coleslaw. It can also serve as a substitute for iceberg lettuce in sandwiches. Cabbage is an excellent source of Vitamin C. Cooked Consumption Cabbage is frequently added to soups and stews. Cabbage soup is particularly popular in Central and Eastern Europe, and the vegetable is a key ingredient in certain types of borscht. It is also widely used in Indian cuisine. Boiling cabbage softens the leaves and releases sugars, which contribute to its characteristic aroma. However, boiled cabbage has been stigmatized in North America due to its strong cooking odor and the perception that it causes flatulence. Despite this, boiled cabbage, when served as a side dish with meats or other foods, can be a valuable source of vitamins and dietary fiber. Stuffed cabbage, a delicacy in Eastern Europe and the Middle East, involves softening the leaves through parboiling or freezing the entire head, then filling them with chopped meat and/or rice. Fermented and Preserved Forms Cabbage serves as the base for German sauerkraut and Korean kimchi. To pickle cabbage, it is placed in a jar, covered with water and salt, and left in a warm environment for several days to ferment. Historically, sauerkraut was prepared in large batches at home as a method of preserving food for the winter. Cabbage can also be pickled in vinegar with various spices, either alone or combined with other vegetables. Korean baechu kimchi is typically sliced thicker than its European counterpart and often includes onions, chilies, minced garlic, and ginger. Medicinal Properties In European folk medicine, cabbage leaves have been used to treat acute inflammation. A paste made from raw cabbage can be wrapped in a cabbage leaf and applied to the affected area to alleviate discomfort. Some claim that cabbage leaves are effective in relieving engorged breasts in breastfeeding women. Cabbage contains significant amounts of glutamine, an amino acid with anti-inflammatory properties. It is also a source of indole-3-carbinol (I3C), a compound used as an adjunct therapy for recurrent respiratory papillomatosis, a disease of the head and neck caused by human papillomavirus (typically types 6 and 11) that leads to airway growths and can be life-threatening. Varieties Cabbage varieties differ in shape and time to maturity. Traditional varieties include Late Flat Dutch, Early Jersey Wakefield (a conical variety), and Danish Ballhead (a late, round-headed type). Savoy cabbage has a round head with crinkled leaves, while red cabbage is a small, round-headed type with dark red leaves. The Krautman variety is commonly used for commercial sauerkraut production. Cultivation Cabbage varieties are broadly categorized into early and late groups. Early varieties mature in approximately 45 days, producing small heads that are best consumed fresh as they do not store well. Late varieties mature in about 87 days and produce larger heads. Cabbage can be started indoors or sown directly. As a cool-season crop, it thrives in early and late plantings rather than in the heat of summer. Controlling insect pests is crucial, especially in commercial production where appearance is a key factor for success. Pesticides such as Sevin and Malathion are approved for use on cabbage. Caterpillars of certain butterflies in the family Pieridae (commonly known as whites) feed on brassicas and can be significant pests. Historically, cabbage was a common winter vegetable due to its ability to store well before the advent of refrigeration and long-distance shipping. China is the leading producer of cabbages, followed by India and the Russian Federation. Related Brassica oleracea Varieties In addition to cabbage, the species Brassica oleracea includes many distinct cultivars commonly known by other names, such as broccoli (Italica Group), cauliflower (Botrytis Group), kale, collard greens, and spring greens (Acephala Group), kohlrabi (Gongylodes Group), Brussels sprouts (Gemmifera Group), Chinese kale or Chinese broccoli (Alboglabra Group), broccolini (Italica × Alboglabra Group), and broccoflower (Italica × Botrytis Group). Linguistic Associations During World War II, the term kraut (cabbage) was used as a racial slur for Germans. In Hebrew, the phrase rosh kruv (cabbage head) implies stupidity. In late 1950s England, French language teachers used the phrase ma petite chou (my little cabbage) as a term of endearment from a man to a woman. Additionally, in England, cabbage is slang for cash, particularly paper money.
